title: Toad in the Hole
subtitle: Yorkshire pudding batter baked around sausages
excerpt: Good pork sausages baked in a crisp Yorkshire pudding batter. A proper British comfort dish that requires a very hot tin and a proper rest of the batter beforehand. The batter must puff dramatically and stay crisp underneath.

recipe.sourceNotes: Toad in the hole has been documented in British cookery since at least the eighteenth century, though early versions used other meats. By the nineteenth century the sausage-and-Yorkshire-pudding combination was standard. The name's origin is disputed; the most common explanation is that the sausages peek out of the batter like toads from holes in the ground.

recipeTools.notes: Large roasting tin, metal, must get very hot.

content.text: Three things matter for toad in the hole: rest the batter for at least an hour; get the tin searingly hot before the batter goes in; and do not open the oven during cooking. The batter must set its rise in the first 15 minutes. Opening the oven will cause it to collapse. The fat in the tin should be smoking before you pour. If it is not hot enough, the batter will not puff properly and will taste doughy underneath.

Make the batter: whisk the flour, salt, and eggs together until smooth. Gradually whisk in the milk and water to make a thin, lump-free batter. Rest for at least 1 hour at room temperature, or up to 24 hours in the fridge.
Heat the oven to 220 C / fan 200 C / gas 7. Put the oil in a large metal roasting tin and heat in the oven for 10 minutes. Add the sausages and cook for 15 minutes, turning once, until browned.

Quickly remove the tin from the oven, arrange the sausages evenly, then immediately pour the rested batter around them. The fat should sizzle and spit. Return to the oven immediately. Do not open the door for 25 minutes.
Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the batter is deeply golden, puffed, and crisp. Serve immediately with onion gravy and mashed potato.
